final.title: Shared logins hide an access-record problem
final.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience choice, not a strategy. For a small business, they create one quiet workflow problem: you lose the record of who has access, who granted it, and who should lose it next. That makes the cost hard to notice until you need to investigate a changed record, recover a deleted file, or remove access after someone leaves.

The manual workaround is familiar: a password list in a note, a spreadsheet, or one person acting as the human router for every account. None of that is elegant. It just keeps the machine running for another week.

If you want a practical next step, ask one question inside the business: who has access to our shared accounts, who gave it to them, and when will they lose it? If nobody can answer cleanly, you have found the real problem.

Then audit the accounts and write down who actually needs access. That gives you a plain baseline before you decide whether the fix is better password management, role-based access, or keeping part of the process manual for now. Shared logins work until they do not, and small teams tend to notice at the least convenient moment.

final.title: Shared logins hide a workflow cost you only see later
final.body:
Shared logins are usually a convenience decision, not a strategy. For an owner-run small business, the quiet cost is simple: you lose the access record. Then it gets hard to tell who changed what, who still has access, and who added the next person. That is not a dramatic failure. It is just the kind that sits there until you need to investigate a mistake or remove access after someone leaves.

The usual workaround is a password note, a spreadsheet, or one person becoming the human router for every account. That keeps the work moving, but it also turns access into memory instead of a process.

The practical next step is a basic audit. Ask: who has access to our shared accounts, who gave it to them, and when should that access end? If no one can answer cleanly, the problem is already visible.

At that point you can decide whether the fix is simple password management, role-based access, or leaving the process manual for now. The main thing is to make the decision on purpose. Shared logins work until they do not, and small teams usually notice the cost at the least convenient moment.
